opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, because I think people sometimes look at a Gaussian splat scene and assume resolution is just a knob you turn. In practice there are a few different constraints stacking on top of each other.

The first is just the representation budget. A splat scene is a big collection of 3D Gaussians, each with a position, covariance, opacity, and some view-dependent color, usually spherical harmonics. If you want finer detail, you generally need more Gaussians, and smaller ones, packed more densely where there's high-frequency content. That scales memory and rendering cost pretty directly. You go from a few million splats to tens of millions, and suddenly you're bounded by GPU memory, by sorting cost in the rasterizer, and by bandwidth if you want to stream the scene to a browser or a headset.

The second is where the information comes from. With classic reconstruction, your resolution ceiling is the input captures. You can't recover detail the cameras never saw, and blur, exposure differences, or slightly wrong camera poses show up as floaters or a soft, smeared look. When you're generating scenes with a model instead of reconstructing them, the ceiling moves to the generative model: what resolution was it trained at, how much 3D-consistent detail can it produce, and can it keep that detail coherent as you move through a large space rather than just one viewpoint.

The third is consistency versus detail. Pushing detail into a single image is relatively easy. Pushing it into a representation that holds up from every angle is much harder, because every bit of fine detail has to be geometrically consistent. A lot of the engineering is figuring out where the detail actually needs to be. Most of a scene doesn't need maximal density, so adaptive allocation, level-of-detail schemes, and smarter densification matter a lot.

Finally, there's the target device. If the goal is something that runs in real time on a phone or in a web viewer, that's a very different budget than an offline render on a big GPU. So much of the question becomes: what's the best visual quality per byte and per millisecond?

So I'd say it's less one hard wall and more a set of tradeoffs between memory, compute, the quality of the underlying data or model, and where you want it to run. All of those are improving quickly, so I'm pretty optimistic the effective resolution of these worlds will keep going up.

r001.rationale: The response says real-time use on a phone or web viewer has a different budget, and explains that more splats increase rendering cost. Together, these clearly identify the device’s real-time budget as a limit on splat rendering.

r002.rationale: The response states that finer detail generally requires more Gaussians packed more densely, linking more splats to higher scene resolution.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few different constraints that stack on top of each other, and it's worth separating them because people tend to conflate them.

The first one is just memory. A Gaussian splat scene is a big unstructured list of primitives, and each one carries position, covariance, opacity, and typically spherical harmonics for view-dependent color. That last part is the killer, because if you go up to third order SH you're carrying something like 48 floats per Gaussian just for appearance. So a scene with a few million Gaussians is already a gigabyte or more. If you want more detail, the naive thing is to add more Gaussians, and that scales linearly in memory. So very quickly you're bumping against the GPU, and that's before you even think about streaming or running this on a phone.

The second constraint is the optimization itself, specifically the densification heuristics. The original 3DGS paper grows the scene by looking at positional gradients and cloning or splitting Gaussians where the gradient is large. That's a heuristic, not a principled thing, and it has failure modes. It tends to under-densify in regions that are far from the cameras or that are textureless, and it can over-densify in regions where the gradients are noisy. So "resolution" in splatting isn't really a global dial you turn, it's an emergent property of where the optimizer decided to put primitives. If you want fine detail in a particular region, you kind of have to trick the densification into caring about that region.

The third thing, and this is the one I find more interesting, is that there's an upper bound set by your input data. These are reconstructions, so you fundamentally can't recover detail that isn't observed in the training images. If your cameras are at a certain distance with a certain sensor, there's a Nyquist-style argument for the finest spatial frequency you can resolve, and adding Gaussians beyond that just lets you overfit to noise. You see this when you zoom in on a splat scene further than any of the training cameras were: it either gets blurry, or you get these little needle-shaped artifacts because the optimizer put in tiny Gaussians to fit pixel-level noise. There was nice work on anti-aliasing, things like Mip-Splatting, that essentially add a low-pass filter so that you render correctly at scales you weren't trained at, and I think that was an important fix. But it's a fix for consistency, not a way to manufacture detail.

And then the fourth constraint, which is more of a representational one, is that Gaussians are a pretty bad basis for sharp edges. A Gaussian is smooth by construction. To represent a crisp boundary you need to stack a lot of them with overlapping tails, and that's wasteful. So some of the recent work on using different kernels, or 2D surfels that are better aligned to surfaces, is really about getting more effective resolution per primitive rather than just more primitives.

So when I think about pushing resolution, the question I'd ask is less "how do I fit more Gaussians" and more "where is the information actually coming from, and what's the most efficient primitive to represent it." Because if the information is there in the images, you can get it with better allocation and better primitives. And if it's not, you need a prior, which basically means a learned model that's hallucinating plausible detail, and at that point you've left reconstruction and you're in generation. Which is fine, that's actually where a lot of the exciting stuff is, but it's a different problem with different failure modes.

r001.rationale: It discusses GPU memory limits and primitive count, but does not identify the target device’s real-time rendering budget as a constraint on how many splats can be rendered.

r002.rationale: It says adding more Gaussians is the naive way to get more detail, directly connecting increased splat count with higher scene resolution.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to separate a couple of things. There’s the resolution you render at, and then there’s the amount of detail actually represented in the scene. You can render more pixels, but if a small feature is represented by one big Gaussian, those extra pixels aren’t going to recover that feature.

To get more detail, you need observations that capture it, and then you need enough Gaussians, placed appropriately, to represent it. That puts pressure on memory and rendering cost. It’s not just the number of Gaussians, either—it’s how much screen space they cover and how many overlap at each pixel.

So I think the interesting question is how to allocate that representation. Where do you need very fine detail, and where can you get away with something coarser? Ideally, as you move closer to something, you’d bring in more detail without having to keep the entire scene at that level all the time.

r001.rationale: It says representation detail puts pressure on rendering cost and notes that overlap and screen coverage affect rendering work, identifying rendering capacity as a constraint on splat count.

r002.rationale: It states that getting more detail requires enough Gaussians placed appropriately, linking more splats to higher scene detail/resolution.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a couple of different constraints that get bundled together when we talk about resolution. One is how much detail you actually captured. If you want to resolve something small in the scene, you need images where that thing occupies enough pixels, ideally from multiple viewpoints. Adding more Gaussians can’t recover detail that was never observed.

Then there’s the representation and the rendering budget. You can use more, smaller Gaussians to represent finer detail, but now you have more parameters to store and more work to render. And the cost depends on the view: how many splats are visible, how much they overlap, and how much of the screen they cover.

So I wouldn’t think of it as just turning up a resolution knob. It’s a question of how you capture the scene, where you allocate capacity, and how you manage detail as the camera moves. Ideally, you spend that capacity on things that actually affect the image at the current viewpoint.
